entries.title: The centroid G: a center of gravity
paragraphs: Archimedes studied the point we call the centroid as the center of gravity of a uniform triangular plate. In Book I, Proposition 13 of On the Equilibrium of Planes, he places this center on a line joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Proposition 14 identifies it as the intersection of two such lines.

The surviving treatise gives an early account of the centroid through the geometry of balance. Our episode establishes concurrence through areas. These propositions document the result; they do not establish when someone first discovered it. Proposition 14 identifies the intersection, rather than stating the familiar 2:1 ratio as its conclusion.

entries.title: The circumcenter O: Euclid’s circle through three vertices
paragraphs: Book IV, Proposition 5 of Euclid’s Elements constructs a circle through the three vertices of a triangle. Euclid bisects two sides and draws perpendiculars through their midpoints. He shows that their intersection is equally distant from the three vertices, so it serves as the center of the required circle.

Euclid considers the intersection inside the triangle, on a side, and outside it. Those cases will be familiar from moving the vertices in our episode. This is a precise ancient account of the circumcenter construction, although Euclid does not use our label O or identify its first discoverer.

entries.title: The orthocenter H: an explicit medieval proof
paragraphs: An explicit proof of altitude concurrence survives in al-Nasawī’s commentary in the Book of Lemmas tradition. Al-Nasawī, active around 1010 CE, starts with the intersection of two altitudes and proves that the line through this point and the third vertex is perpendicular to the opposite side. Jan Hogendijk’s edition and English translation let us read this argument directly.

The translated passage identifies this auxiliary lemma as al-Nasawī’s. It is distinct from al-Kūhī’s circle theorems discussed in the same article. The Book of Lemmas traditionally bears Archimedes’ name, but that tradition does not establish that Archimedes wrote the surviving compilation. This is a documented early proof, with no claim here that al-Nasawī was the first discoverer.

entries.title: The incenter I: Euclid’s inscribed circle
paragraphs: Immediately before his circumcircle construction, Euclid constructs the incircle in Elements IV.4. He intersects two internal angle bisectors, drops perpendiculars to the three sides, and uses congruent right triangles to show that those perpendicular distances are equal. A circle with that common radius touches all three sides.

Euclid presents a circle construction. The modern statement that the three internal angle bisectors meet at the incenter expresses the same geometry using the angle-bisector characterization. The proposition is an early surviving source for the construction; it makes no claim to identify its original discoverer.

entries.title: The Euler line: three centers in one relation
paragraphs: Euler’s Solutio facilis problematum quorundam geometricorum difficillimorum studies the relations among triangle centers. For a non-equilateral triangle, it establishes that the circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter lie on one line, with the centroid dividing the circumcenter–orthocenter segment in the ratio 1:2. In our notation, GH = 2GO.

The Euler Archive dates the paper’s composition to 1763 and its publication to 1767. The date 1765 often attached to this result is the year assigned to the journal volume. Euler’s labels also differ from ours: his E, F, H correspond to our H, G, O. Our episode’s constructed point X and similar triangles are a modern presentation of the relation, not a transcription of his argument.

entries.title: The angle-bisector theorem, including its converse
paragraphs: The angle-bisector theorem appears explicitly in Elements VI.3. Euclid states both directions: an internal angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides, and that ratio conversely identifies the bisector. His argument introduces a parallel line and compares the resulting segments.

This gives us a precise ancient text to read alongside the episode’s area argument. The theorem and its converse were already presented together in the Elements. As with the circle constructions, the surviving account does not establish that Euclid was the first person to discover the result.

entries.title: The right angle in a semicircle: a theorem and a later attribution
entries.period: Aristotle · Fourth century BCE; Euclid · Around 300 BCE
paragraphs: The right angle in a semicircle was already a familiar example in Aristotle’s fourth-century BCE writings. Posterior Analytics II.11 discusses why this angle is right. Euclid later gives a systematic geometric proof in Elements III.31.

The name Thales’ theorem rests on a different kind of evidence. Writing many centuries after Thales, Diogenes Laertius reports Pamphila’s claim that Thales first inscribed a right triangle in a circle; he also records a competing attribution to Pythagoras. That passage supplies neither a proof by Thales nor an explicit statement about a diameter. It preserves a later attribution, rather than securely identifying the theorem’s first discovery.

entries.title: The nine-point circle: all nine points in an 1821 paper
paragraphs: Brianchon and Poncelet’s Théorème IX gives an explicit early statement and proof of the full nine-point theorem. It includes the three altitude feet, three side midpoints, and three midpoints between the orthocenter and vertices. Their article appeared in the issue dated 1 January 1821. All nine points are already present together in that publication.

The theorem there concerns the nine points lying on one circle; it does not state the center and radius in the form used in our episodes. Feuerbach’s 1822 book develops further properties of the circle, including its center midway between the circumcenter and orthocenter. Earlier related investigations make a single first-discovery claim difficult. The sources below document particular statements and distinguish them from the later history of the name.

entries.title: Ceva’s theorem before Ceva
paragraphs: The theorem named after Giovanni Ceva has an earlier surviving account in the Book of Perfection of al-Muʾtaman ibn Hūd, ruler of Zaragoza. Jan Hogendijk identifies the concurrency criterion, including both directions, as Proposition 312.18 in the surviving manuscript tradition. Whether al-Muʾtaman devised it or drew on an unidentified source is unresolved.

Ceva published the ratio relation in De lineis rectis in 1678. His book connects geometry with balancing weights; it also prints an area argument credited to Pietro Paolo Caravaggio the younger. That makes a useful comparison with our episode’s areas. These records do not establish a route of transmission from al-Muʾtaman to Ceva, but they show why a theorem’s name need not identify its earliest surviving appearance.

The trigonometric episode expresses the same concurrency criterion using sines of angles. Venema states this form in §8.4 of his 2013 text. That modern formulation is the source cited for the new episode; the early accounts above concern the side-ratio criterion and are not presented here as sources for this exact trigonometric statement.

entries.title: The symmedian point: a modern terminology reference
paragraphs: Venema defines a symmedian as the isogonal of a median: reflect the median line through the internal angle bisector at its vertex. He calls the common point of the three symmedians the symmedian point and denotes it by K; it is the isogonal conjugate of the centroid.

This reference documents the terminology and characterization used in the episode. It is a modern exposition, not an early historical source, and it does not by itself identify the first use of the name or the first proof of concurrence.

entries.title: Nagel and Gergonne: the names of two contact-point centers
entries.period: Nineteenth-century names · Modern account in Venema
paragraphs: Venema names the Nagel point after the German geometer Christian Heinrich von Nagel (1803–1882), and the Gergonne point after the French mathematician Joseph Diaz Gergonne (1771–1859). These are attributions of the centers’ names in a modern textbook.

His construction of the Gergonne point joins each vertex to the opposite incircle contact; his construction of the Nagel point uses the opposite excircle contact instead. The episodes explain concurrence using Ceva’s theorem. The cited passage supplies the names and constructions, but it does not establish a first publication or first-discovery claim.

entries.title: Heron’s formula: its name and the proof used here
entries.period: Ancient attribution · Modern exposition in Venema
paragraphs: Venema introduces the area formula under the name of Heron of Alexandria, the ancient Greek geometer. His discussion treats the traditional attribution separately from the argument developed in the section; the name alone does not settle the formula’s first discovery.

The episode follows Venema’s modern incircle-and-excircle proof, with equal tangent lengths and two pairs of similar right triangles. This identifies the source of this particular classroom argument. It does not present that argument as a transcription of an ancient proof by Heron.

entries.title: Inscribed angles and cyclic quadrilaterals
paragraphs: Book III of Euclid’s Elements relates angles at the circumference to angles at the center in Proposition 20. Proposition 21 compares angles in the same segment, and Proposition 22 proves that opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary.

These are early surviving accounts of the angle facts used here. Our cyclic-quadrilateral episode also proves the converse; that converse is not the statement of Proposition 22. The intercepted arc must be identified when the corresponding central angle is reflex.

entries.title: Power of a point: products of segments
paragraphs: Euclid’s Elements III.35 proves equality of the products cut off by intersecting chords. Proposition III.36 relates the product along an exterior secant to the square of a tangent segment.

The modern signed quantity OP² − R² packages the interior and exterior cases into one definition. Euclid states the results in terms of rectangles and squares, rather than this modern signed notation. The episode keeps the positive chord product inside the circle distinct from the negative signed power.

entries.title: Ptolemy: a quadrilateral identity for chords
paragraphs: The Almagest develops a relation between the diagonals and opposite sides of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle as part of its treatment of chords. In Halma’s Greek–French edition, the statement and auxiliary-angle construction begin on printed page 29 of volume I.

This gives a precise surviving location for the theorem bearing Ptolemy’s name. It is not a claim that the surviving record determines its first discovery. Our notation labels the fourth vertex D and the auxiliary point X.

sources.title: Ptolemy, Almagest, Book I, chapter 10

entries.title: Brahmagupta: the area of a cyclic quadrilateral
paragraphs: Brahmagupta’s Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta treats the area and diagonals of cyclic quadrilaterals. Satyanad Kichenassamy’s historical analysis reads propositions XII.21–27 as a connected derivation and discusses the diagonal formula that follows in XII.28.

The episode gives a modern proof using supplementary angles, triangle areas, and a cosine-law lemma derived from Pythagoras. It does not claim to reproduce Brahmagupta’s argument. The formula is stated for convex cyclic quadrilaterals; a zero side belongs to a limiting degeneration, not that domain.
